areas.blurb: The Code tab, feature by feature.

areas.title: App Development
areas.blurb: Build a small app from idea to production.

areas.title: Process
areas.blurb: From idea to deploy, with gates.

areas.title: Workflow
areas.blurb: Rules, memory, skills, hooks and automation.

articles.title: Tour of the Code Tab
articles.covers: Orient a new user in the Code tab: the session list in the sidebar with + New (Cmd+N), the conversation view, the prompt box with the project folder row beneath it, the permission mode, model and effort controls, and the panes. Name each area as the docs do and say which later article covers it.

articles.title: Install, Sign In and Your First Session
articles.covers: Install the desktop app, sign in, and run a first session in the Trail Notes starter folder: choose the folder, send a prompt that asks Claude to explain the project, read the tool calls and approvals as they appear, and stop a session. Point to the Terminal install article for the CLI.

articles.title: Sessions and the Sidebar
articles.covers: A session is an independent conversation with its own history, folder, context and changes. Cover + New and Cmd+N, Ctrl+Tab to cycle, Group and sort, rename by clicking the title, archive and the Archived list, auto-archive after a PR is merged or closed. Pinning and searching the sidebar are seen in the app but not in the docs: use the Observed in the app callout.

articles.title: Choosing a Project Folder
articles.covers: The folder row under the prompt box, how the folder shapes what Claude can read and change, and the environment selector for local, cloud and SSH sessions (cloud sessions pick repositories). Scratch workspaces appear in the app but are not in the docs: use the Observed in the app callout and tell readers to pick a real folder for real work.

articles.title: Permission Modes Explained
articles.covers: The desktop modes: Manual, Accept edits, Plan, Auto and Bypass permissions, what each allows without asking, where the control sits under the prompt box. dontAsk is CLI-only. Auto needs Opus 4.6 or later, Sonnet 4.6 or later, Haiku 5.5 or a Fable model, and admins can turn it off. The author runs Auto almost always, backed by hooks and rules (see usage audit).

articles.title: The Panes: Changes, Files, Terminal, Browser, Tasks
articles.covers: Chat, Changes, Browser, Terminal, Files, Plan, Background tasks and Subagent panes, plus the iOS Simulator pane (public beta, macOS, local sessions). Drag to rearrange, pop a pane out and dock it back. Cmd+Shift+B toggles the Browser pane. Note that computer use is a separate research-preview feature. The Plan pane's contents are not described in the docs.

articles.title: Worktrees and Branches in the App
articles.covers: The worktree toggle (off by default), worktrees in <project>/.claude/worktrees/, the branch prefix setting, .worktreeinclude for ignored files you still need, why a worktree per session avoids collisions, and cleaning up when the work merges. Half the author's sessions ran in worktrees.

articles.title: Pull Requests and Auto-fix
articles.covers: CI check status in the Changes card, Auto-fix (Claude fixes failing checks and addresses review comments from owners, members, collaborators or GitHub Apps in local sessions), Merge when ready (GitHub auto-merge, squash by default unless a merge queue is used, disabled in SSH and WSL), and the CLI counterpart /autofix-pr. State what Auto-fix will not decide for you.

articles.title: Customize: Skills, Plugins and Connectors
articles.covers: The Customize area: skills (load automatically or invoke with /; personal, project, plugin and claude.ai-synced), plugins (+ then Add plugins; scopes user, project, local; not in cloud or WSL sessions) and connectors (MCP servers with guided setup, + then Add connectors). Include how to audit what you installed.

articles.title: Split View, Side Chat and Side Sessions
articles.covers: Split view (Option or Alt-click a session, or right-click then Open in then Split view, Cmd+Ctrl+W to take it out), side chat (Cmd+; or /btw, not saved after you close the app), suggested tasks (Start, Do it here, Options, Start all), and Claude working across your other sessions (list, read, message, rename, archive). The author started 217 side sessions.

articles.title: Remote Control and Cloud Sessions
articles.covers: Remote Control connects a local session to claude.ai/code and your other devices (per session or with /remote-control; Trusted Devices is beta). Cloud sessions run on Anthropic-managed infrastructure and continue after you close the app, with modes Accept edits, Plan and Auto, and view-only Files. Say when each fits.

articles.title: Projects, Dispatch and Artifacts
articles.covers: Projects (public beta, Pro and Max, rolling out gradually) track many cloud sessions from one conversation. Dispatch is a persistent Cowork conversation that can start Code sessions (Pro or Max only, setup in a support article). Artifacts are live pages published to claude.ai (templates are beta). Label each one exactly and say who can use it.

articles.title: Prompting for Results
articles.covers: State the goal, the constraints and how you will know it worked. Give context with files and screenshots you attach to the prompt box. Ask for a plan before big changes. Iterate in small corrections. In the author's transcripts about 1% of prompts begin with a negation word, which is a sign the first prompt carried enough context.

articles.title: Plan Mode: Think Before You Edit
articles.covers: Plan mode explores and proposes before editing. In the app, choose Plan in the permission mode control under the prompt box. Terminal: /plan, Shift+Tab to cycle modes, claude --permission-mode plan, and the opusplan model alias. The author never enters plan mode and plans with the task list and spec skills instead, so show both and say when each fits.

articles.title: Reading and Reviewing Diffs
articles.covers: Open the Changes pane, review file by file, click a line to comment, and ask for another pass. Teach a reading order: tests first, then the smallest files, then the logic. What to look for in an AI-written diff: unrequested changes, deleted tests, new dependencies.

articles.title: Undo and Recover
articles.covers: /rewind restores the conversation and/or code to an earlier point. Git is the real safety net: commit before big changes, and know git status, git diff, git restore and git revert. Say to read the checkpointing page for what it does and does not track. Worktrees as a cheap way to throw work away.

articles.title: Debugging with Claude
articles.covers: Reproduce first. Give Claude the exact error and how to trigger it. Ask for hypotheses ranked by likelihood before any change, make the smallest fix, then add a regression test. The bundled /debug skill. Use the Trail Notes seeded bug in notes.js as the worked example.

articles.title: Refactoring Safely
articles.covers: Tests before refactor, small steps, a worktree or branch, a diff review after every step, and behavior that must not change written down first. The bundled /simplify skill. Show a Trail Notes refactor that extracts storage from app.js.

articles.title: Test-Driven Development with Claude
articles.covers: Red, green, refactor with Claude. Ask for one failing test first, run it and confirm it fails for the right reason, then the smallest code to pass, then a refactor. Use zero-dependency node:test or plain assert scripts from Trail Notes. How to stop Claude from editing tests to make them pass.

articles.title: Code Review, Yours and Claude's
articles.covers: Review your own diff in the Changes pane, run the bundled /code-review skill, and ask a fresh subagent for an adversarial read that has not seen your reasoning. /ultrareview is a research preview, and its page says the command is /code-review ultra. Treat Claude's findings as leads to verify, not verdicts.

articles.title: Security Review Habits
articles.covers: A quick threat-model pass per change, secrets never pasted into prompts or files, deny rules and hooks for destructive commands, and treating text from web pages, files and tool output as data and not instructions. A human reads security-critical code (auth, payments, data deletion) line by line.

articles.title: Scoping an App Before You Build
articles.covers: Who it is for, the one job it does, the smallest slice that proves it, and the non-goals. Have Claude interview you one question at a time and write a one-page brief. Worked example: Trail Notes in one page.

articles.title: Spec First: Grilling and a Glossary
articles.covers: Run a grilling session until every decision is explicit, record terms in a glossary (including terms to avoid), write short decision records for hard-to-reverse choices, then turn the spec into tickets that declare what blocks what. Pattern 10 in patterns-from-practice.

articles.title: Choosing a Stack for a Small App
articles.covers: A decision table: static files plus a few serverless functions, no build step, when to add a framework, free hosting that needs no card, and how to ask Claude to argue against your choice. The author's apps are framework-free PWAs (pattern 14). Tell readers to check current free-tier terms themselves.

articles.title: A Static PWA on a Free Host
articles.covers: A web manifest, a service worker in outline, HTTPS, and deploying a static folder to a free host. Use the Trail Notes starter. Verify host specifics against the host's own docs and keep them minimal.

articles.title: UI and Design Systems with Claude
articles.covers: Tokens before components, a screenshot loop using the Browser pane, contrast and keyboard checks, and light and dark mode. This site's own design system (docs/design-system.md) is the case study. Ask Claude to critique against a named checklist, not to make it prettier.

articles.title: Testing Without a Framework
articles.covers: Zero-dependency checks: node:assert and node:test, one runner that runs every check file, a pre-push hook that runs the same runner, and CI that repeats it. Use exercises/trail-notes-starter/checks. Pattern 15.

articles.title: Preview, Ship and Maintain
articles.covers: Preview in the Browser pane (Dev servers menu, launch.json for preview servers, the autoVerify setting), the iOS Simulator pane (public beta, macOS, local sessions only, for native iOS work), deploying a verified commit, and a light maintenance rhythm.

articles.title: Backend Pieces: Functions, KV, D1 and R2
articles.covers: What serverless functions, a key-value store, a SQL database and object storage are each for, how to choose between them, and a safe workflow for schema changes with Claude (write the migration, read it, run it on a copy first). Use the platform's own docs for specifics, cite them, and keep it brief.

articles.title: Offline-First with Service Workers
articles.covers: Cache the app shell, keep data in IndexedDB or a baked-in seed, version the cache, and add a gate that fails when the cached asset list changes without a version bump (pattern 8). Use the Trail Notes solution for capstone 3a. Test by going offline in the Browser pane.

articles.title: Auth: Access and Passkeys
articles.covers: An access layer in front of the app versus passkeys (WebAuthn) inside it, what each protects, what Claude can draft, and why a human reads every line of auth code. Never paste secrets into a prompt. Verify specifics against the provider's docs.

articles.title: AI Features Safely: Retrieval versus Generation
articles.covers: When search over a document corpus beats generating an answer, how to keep a language model out of the answer path when accuracy matters, a fixed benchmark that every change must not lower (pattern 9), and how to make the tool say it does not know. Use an anonymized technician-search example.

articles.title: The Idea-to-Deploy Flow
articles.covers: The whole path on one page with a diagram: idea, grill, spec, tickets, branch or worktree, build with checks, pull request and CI, merge, deploy the exact commit, record it. Say what each step guards against.

articles.title: Grill, Spec, Tickets
articles.covers: How to run the grilling session, what a spec contains, and how tickets declare what blocks what so work can run in parallel. Link the spec and plan templates. Include a Trail Notes tags feature as the example.

articles.title: One Branch per Change
articles.covers: Branch names, one worktree per change, small pull requests, keeping a branch current with main, and deleting branch and worktree after the merge. The author's cost is stale worktrees, so cleanup is part of the process.

articles.title: Definition of Done and Gates
articles.covers: Write down what done means, then enforce it with checks that fail loudly. Gates that check gates (pattern 8), a pre-push hook that runs the same checks as CI, and the rule that a skipped check is a failed check.

articles.title: Pull Requests That Review Fast
articles.covers: Small diffs, a body that says what changed and what was verified and what was not, a self-review in the Changes pane first, and a /code-review pass. Link the PR body template.

articles.title: CI That Gates the Deploy
articles.covers: A GitHub Actions workflow that runs the checks on every push and pull request, and a deploy workflow that depends on them. Deploy the exact commit by packaging a ref with git archive, then read the deploy log. Mention anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 as an option. Use GitHub's own docs for workflow syntax.

articles.title: A Standing Go with a Stop List
articles.covers: How to write a rule that lets Claude merge and deploy when work is ready, the conditions that define ready, and the stop list that always returns the decision to you. Use gh pr merge with --match-head-commit. Add the typed-phrase guard for the one action that must never be automatic (patterns 2 and 3).

articles.title: Handoff Ledgers and Retros
articles.covers: A ledger file that records each deploy with the commit, version, what was verified and what was not, why it grows unreadable, and how to rotate it. A short retro after incidents. Link the handoff and retro templates (patterns 6 and 4).

articles.title: How Context Works
articles.covers: What fills the context window (your prompts, file reads, tool output, subagent results), what /context shows, what auto-compaction does, and why long sessions get worse. No numbers beyond what the docs print. 94 of the author's 498 sessions exceed 500 records.

articles.title: Clear, Compact and Hand Off
articles.covers: /clear starts clean, /compact [instructions] summarizes, and a handoff note you write carries what matters into a fresh session. The author uses handoffs and /clear and almost never /compact. A hook that warns at 70% and 90% is a pattern worth copying (pattern 4). /rewind as the fourth option.

articles.title: Model and Effort Trade-offs
articles.covers: Pick a model with Cmd+Shift+I and effort with Cmd+Shift+E. Levels are low, medium, high, xhigh and max, and supported levels vary by model. The opusplan alias. A method for choosing: start lower, raise effort when work comes back shallow, and check /usage. The author mostly runs xhigh. Do not state prices or speeds.

articles.title: Delegating to Subagents
articles.covers: Built-in subagents are Explore, Plan and General-purpose. Delegation keeps the main thread lean because only the conclusion returns. The Background tasks pane shows running subagents. Delegate by a count, such as more than three files to read (pattern 5). The author's usage: general-purpose 1,194 calls, scout 120.

articles.title: Reading Your Usage, Context and Skills
articles.covers: /usage (aliases /cost and /stats), /context, and /skill-doctor (v2.1.252 or later), which shows each skill's context cost and flags skills you never invoke. OpenTelemetry metrics for teams, with traces in beta. What to look at weekly.

articles.title: Fast Mode: When It Pays
articles.covers: /fast toggles a faster configuration for Claude Opus at higher per-token cost. It is a research preview, and the docs cover the CLI and cloud sessions, not the Desktop page. The author has never used it. Teach how to decide and how to measure whether it helped, without stating prices. Use the Observed in the app callout for the Desktop tab.

articles.title: Profiling and Benchmarking with Claude
articles.covers: Measure first, form a hypothesis, change one thing, measure again. Claude writes the harness and you read the numbers. Free tools only (Node's built-in profiler, browser devtools). Verify any flag with node --help. Trail Notes list rendering with a thousand notes as the example.

articles.title: Measure a Workflow Before and After
articles.covers: Pick metrics you can collect: permission prompts per session, corrections per session, context percentage at handoff, time to a green check. Change one thing, re-measure, keep or revert. Use the author's aggregates as a baseline example and the exercises/messy-workflow worksheet.

articles.title: A CLAUDE.md That Earns Its Keep
articles.covers: CLAUDE.md is loaded at session start for project and user levels. Keep it short (the author's are 13 to 20 lines), write rules in words Claude can follow, and move bulky material into files it can read on demand. /memory opens the files. Link the CLAUDE.md template.

articles.title: Rules and Global Settings
articles.covers: User-level instructions and settings that apply to every project. Settings precedence from highest: managed, --settings, settings.local.json, settings.json, user settings.json. The author's pattern of eight small rules files, one rule each (pattern 1). Link the rules-file template.

articles.title: Memory: What to Save
articles.covers: Auto memory is on by default in local sessions and toggles with /memory. What is worth keeping (corrections you gave, project decisions, pointers to external resources) and what is not (anything the code already shows). Periodic cleanup. The author has 269 memory files across 15 projects.

articles.title: Your First Skill
articles.covers: A skill is a SKILL.md folder invoked as /skill-name or loaded automatically. Cover locations, the frontmatter fields the docs name, and writing the description so it triggers. Audit with /skill-doctor. Build a small skill for Trail Notes. Link the skill template.

articles.title: Permission Tuning for Fewer Prompts
articles.covers: Allow, ask and deny rules such as Bash(npm test), working directories, and when Auto mode is the better answer. A method: list the read-only commands you approve repeatedly and allow only those. The author has no allow list and runs Auto. State the trade-off honestly.

articles.title: Subagents by Design
articles.covers: Custom agents live in .claude/agents/ and /agents. One purpose each, a tool allowlist, a defined return format, and isolation: worktree for risky work. Two shapes from the author's setup: a read-only scout, and a memory auditor that proposes edits and never applies them. Agent teams are experimental and off by default. Link the subagent template.

articles.title: Hooks: Guardrails and Warnings
articles.covers: 33 hook events and five handler types (command, http, mcp_tool, prompt, agent; agent is experimental). Four shapes from the author's setup: block destructive git commands on PreToolUse for Bash, warn at context thresholds after tool use, re-arm after PostCompact, and report drift on SessionStart. Read the hooks page for exact input, output and exit-code behavior before writing any claim. Link the hook template.

articles.title: Parallel Sessions Without Collisions
articles.covers: One worktree per session, one writer per set of files, split view to watch two sessions, the Background tasks pane, and how many sessions you can supervise. Cleaning up. The author's second week started 209 sessions.

articles.title: Handoffs Between Sessions and Devices
articles.covers: A handoff note carries intent, state, decisions and next steps into a fresh session. Resume with /resume or claude -r. Remote Control continues a local session from another device. The author keeps a private repository of handoff notes to move work between machines. Link the handoff template.

articles.title: Config as a Repo
articles.covers: Keep your user-level Claude configuration in a repository with symlinks, a manifest of pinned vendored packages, a session-start hook that warns on drift, and backups (pattern 12). Never commit identifiers, tokens or personal data. Say what belongs in the folder using the docs' description of it.

articles.title: Scheduled Tasks and Loops
articles.covers: Desktop scheduled tasks run on your machine only while the app is open and the computer is awake, and each run is a new session. Cloud scheduled tasks (formerly routines) are a research preview. /loop repeats a prompt while a session stays open and /schedule manages cloud tasks. Use the author's chores as examples (pattern 13).

articles.title: Start a New Project
articles.covers: From an empty folder to a first commit: create the folder, git init, a CLAUDE.md, a first prompt for the skeleton, a check script, a first commit. Use the Trail Notes starter. Steps in the app, with Terminal tips for git.

articles.title: Ship a Feature End to End
articles.covers: Add tags to Trail Notes: spec, worktree and branch, a failing check, the change, the diff review, a pull request, CI, merge. This is the recipe behind capstone 2.

articles.title: Fix a Bug from a Report
articles.covers: Turn a vague report into a reproduction, a failing test, a minimal fix and a pull request that says what was and was not verified. Use the seeded Trail Notes bug.

articles.title: Audit an Unfamiliar Repo
articles.covers: Map a repo you did not write without flooding your context: a read-only subagent returns the layout, the commands to run, the risky areas and the tests. Then you read only what matters.

articles.title: Migrate a Dependency
articles.covers: Read the changelog first, pin the target version, run the checks before touching anything, migrate in small steps in a worktree, and keep a rollback. Keep it generic and use the Node standard library or a simple pinned tool as the example.

articles.title: Which Permission Mode
articles.covers: A decision table for Manual, Accept edits, Plan, Auto and Bypass permissions by task risk and how much you trust the checks around you.

articles.title: Plan Mode or Not
articles.covers: When plan mode earns its extra step, when a task list or a spec is better, and when to skip planning entirely.

articles.title: New Session or Continue
articles.covers: A decision table for continuing, using /clear, writing a handoff and starting fresh, based on how unrelated the next task is and how full the context is.

articles.title: Which Model and Effort
articles.covers: A decision table that starts low and raises effort or model when the work comes back shallow, with fast mode as a separate question. No prices or speed claims.

articles.title: Skill, Subagent or Hook
articles.covers: Use a skill to teach Claude a procedure, a subagent to keep heavy work out of the main thread, a hook to enforce something every time, and a rule in CLAUDE.md for a preference. A table with an example of each.

articles.title: Long Sessions and Context Rot
articles.covers: Symptoms of a bloated session (forgotten instructions, repeated mistakes, slow progress) and fixes in order: /context to look, /clear or a handoff, a subagent for heavy reading.

articles.title: Claude Ignores My Instructions
articles.covers: Why an instruction gets lost (too long, buried, contradicted, not loaded) and how to check what was loaded, tighten it, move it to a hook if it must always happen.

articles.title: Permission Prompt Fatigue
articles.covers: Too many approval prompts: find the repeated ones, allow the safe read-only commands, consider Auto, and keep deny rules for the dangerous ones. Measure prompts per session before and after.

articles.title: Errors and Retries
articles.covers: Tool errors versus API errors, what to try first (retry, claude doctor, update, resume), when an error means a bad command and when it means a service problem. The author saw 1,606 tool errors and 792 API errors in four weeks and most sessions finished anyway.

articles.title: Worktree Sprawl
articles.covers: Stale worktrees pile up (about 25 and 16 in two of the author's projects). List them with git worktree list, remove merged ones, and make cleanup part of the merge step.

articles.title: Install and Update
articles.covers: Open Terminal and learn cd, ls and pwd. Install with the native installer or brew install --cask, sign in with /login, update with claude update, check with claude doctor. Explain what the installer one-liner does and that readers can inspect a script before running it. Do not show output you did not see.

articles.title: Core Flags and Modes
articles.covers: Only flags present in CLI 2.1.304 help: --model, --effort, --permission-mode, --name or -n, -c, -r, -w, --add-dir. A table of what each does. Do not teach documented flags that are missing from the help.

articles.title: Resume and Continue
articles.covers: claude -c continues the latest session, claude -r picks one, /resume searches by title, folder or branch, and --fork-session branches a conversation. When to use each.

articles.title: git and gh Essentials
articles.covers: The few git commands that matter (status, diff, add, commit, switch, log, restore) and the gh commands for pull requests (pr create, pr view, pr checks, pr merge) plus gh auth status and gh auth switch for more than one account. Link GitHub's own docs. Explain each command.

articles.title: Headless and Scripting
articles.covers: claude -p runs one prompt non-interactively. Cover --output-format (text, json, stream-json), --json-schema, --max-budget-usd, --allowedTools and --continue. Pointers to the Agent SDK and GitHub Actions. --max-turns is documented but absent from 2.1.304 help, so do not teach it.
